name: Rock 'n' Roll
def: R&B accelerated for a teenage mass market — sharper backbeat, guitar hooks and rebellion packaged as pop. The first youth-culture genre.

traits.v: Hard backbeat and a driving shuffle.
Electric guitar hooks, piano, upright or electric bass.
Tight two- to three-minute verse-chorus singles.

why: It speeds R&B's shuffle and backbeat into hook-driven singles built for teenagers.

tracks.why: Berry's double-stop intro riff codified the electric-guitar vocabulary of rock.

name: Rockabilly
def: Southern rock 'n' roll built from hillbilly country and R&B — slapback echo, slapped upright bass, twangy electric lead and hiccupping vocals, cut largely at Sam Phillips' Sun Records in Memphis.

traits.v: Slapback tape echo on voice and guitar.
Slapped upright bass driving a fast two-beat shuffle, often with sparse or no drums.
Hiccups, stutters and yelps.
Sun Records, Memphis, mid-1950s.

why: It plays country's instrumentation and twang at R&B's tempo and attack — the 'billy' strand of rock 'n' roll.

tracks.why: His 1954 Sun debut: an Arthur Crudup blues played with a country trio's slap bass and slapback echo.

name: Psychobilly
def: Rockabilly rebuilt with punk speed and B-movie horror — slapped double bass, reverb-drenched guitar and lyrics about monsters, zombies and the grave.

traits.v: Rockabilly shuffle at punk tempo, driven by a fast, clicking slapped upright bass.
Twangy, heavily reverbed guitar with fuzz and surf echo.
Snarls, yelps and horror-host howls.
London's Klub Foot and the Meteors' 'wreckin' crew'; quiffs and flat-tops.

why: It keeps rockabilly's slap bass and twang but plays them with punk's speed and aggression, swapping teen romance for horror-film camp.

tracks.why: The 1978 single that set the template: rockabilly stomp, garage fuzz and B-movie lyrics.

name: Progressive Rock
def: Rock scaled to classical ambition — suite-length compositions, odd meters, virtuoso playing and concept albums as complete statements.

traits.v: Multi-part suites and side-long epics.
Odd meters and through-composed shifts.
Mellotron, organ and synth beside virtuoso guitar.
The album as artwork; post-psychedelic ambition.

why: It stretches rock into through-composed, odd-metered suites where virtuosity and form outrank the single.

albums.t: In the Court of the Crimson King

tracks.why: Its jazz-metal fury and stop-time precision announced prog’s ambitions in one track.

tempoNote: Highly variable — suite-length pieces shift tempo and meter constantly.

name: Garage Rock
def: Raw, amateur, primal rock made by teenage bands in suburban garages — distortion, attitude and three chords over polish.

traits.v: Distorted, lo-fi, untreated guitar.
Blunt, driving eighth-note pulse.
Suburban teenage amateurism.

why: It strips rock to three raw chords and amateur energy, making imperfection itself the sound.

name: Beat / British Invasion
def: The self-contained British guitar group — rock 'n' roll, skiffle and R&B compressed into two guitars, bass, drums and shared harmony. Merseybeat swept Britain in 1963; in February 1964 the Beatles took it to America and reset pop.

traits.v: Two electric guitars, bass and drums — the band writes and plays everything.
Hook-first two-minute songcraft with close two- and three-part harmony.
A driving, even backbeat — the "beat" itself.
Liverpool's Cavern Club and Hamburg residencies; the 1964 Invasion of the US charts.

why: It turns American rock 'n' roll and R&B into the self-contained, harmony-singing guitar band that writes its own hooks — the template for nearly every rock group after.

tracks.why: The 1963 single at the heart of Beatlemania — harmony, backbeat and hook in two minutes twenty.

name: Power Pop
def: The 1964–66 beat-group sound kept alive and amplified — chiming guitars, Beatlesque harmony and three-minute hooks played with hard-rock muscle. Pete Townshend coined the term in 1967; Badfinger, Raspberries and Big Star made it a genre in the early 70s.

traits.v: Concise, major-key hooks under stacked Beatlesque harmony.
Big overdriven chords beneath chiming, often twelve-string, guitar.
Tight verse-chorus singles — three minutes, no jamming.
A commercial failure in its own time — Big Star barely sold, then became canon.

why: It preserves the beat group's melodic economy while borrowing hard rock's wattage — pop craft at rock volume.

tracks.why: Chiming twelve-string, aching harmony and a perfect chorus — the genre's sacred text.

name: Skinny-Tie Power Pop
def: Power pop's late-70s chart moment — punk-tightened tempos, bright radio polish and skinny ties, cresting with The Knack's 'My Sharona' in the summer of 1979.

traits.v: Punk-era drive — faster, tighter and more nervous than the early-70s wave.
Bright, compressed late-70s radio sheen.
Handclap choruses, harmonies and songs about girls.
LA and Midwest club scenes and the major-label power pop gold rush of 1979.

why: It plays power pop's hooks at punk's tempo with new wave's polish — the style's one genuine mass-market wave.

tracks.why: Arena-sized power pop — the bridge between Big Star's cult and the 1979 chart wave.

name: Power Pop Revival
def: The indie generation rediscovers Big Star — Teenage Fanclub's Bandwagonesque and Matthew Sweet's Girlfriend in 1991, Jellyfish and The Posies alongside, Weezer and Fountains of Wayne carrying the songbook through the decade.

traits.v: Big Star worship — chime, harmony and ache, now with 90s guitar crunch.
Alt-rock weight under classicist songcraft.
Indie labels, college radio and the Big Star reissue canon.

why: It reclaims power pop's 70s songbook through indie rock's sound and distribution, turning a commercial failure into a permanent canon.

tracks.why: Bandwagonesque topped Spin's 1991 albums of the year over Nevermind — Big Star chime under grunge-era fuzz.

name: Sunshine Pop
def: California's bright, orchestrated harmony pop — stacked mixed-voice vocals, lush Wrecking Crew arrangements and folk-pop songcraft radiating mid-60s LA optimism.

traits.v: Dense, stacked male–female harmony, four and five parts deep.
Strings, horns and woodwinds over LA session-pro rhythm tracks.
Sweet, major-seventh-tinted and relentlessly sunny.
LA studios, 1966–69 — the soft flipside of the psychedelic era.

why: It takes beat and folk-rock harmony singing to orchestral, studio-built heights — optimism as an arrangement style.

tracks.why: Five-part harmony over a Wrecking Crew track — the sunshine sound at its 1967 peak.

name: Bubblegum Pop
def: Singles-factory pop aimed at pre-teens — Kasenetz-Katz and Buddah Records studio concoctions and cartoon bands built on a bouncing beat, nursery-rhyme hooks and candy metaphors; The Archies' 'Sugar, Sugar' was Billboard's #1 single of 1969.

traits.v: One chanted, singalong hook — the whole point of the record.
Bouncy, square, danceable beat.
Anonymous session hands; the "band" is often a cartoon or a brand.
Buddah Records, Saturday-morning TV and the pre-teen singles market, 1967–72.

why: It strips the beat group to pure hook and manufacture — proof the chorus alone can carry a record, a lesson glam and pop-punk both learned.

tracks.why: A cartoon band's session-singer confection that outsold everything in 1969.

name: Psychedelic Rock
def: Rock expanded by the studio and the trip — modal jams, drones, tape effects and extended, exploratory arrangements.

traits.v: Fuzz, phasing, sitar and organ drones, studio tape effects.
Modal vamps and drone-based, non-functional progressions.
Extended, improvisatory jams and suite-like forms.

why: Modal, drone-anchored jamming and heavy studio processing trade pop concision for hypnotic, exploratory texture.

albums.t: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn

tempoNote: Variable — extended jams drift across tempos.

name: Hard Rock
def: Electric blues turned up to arena scale — riff-led, swaggering rock built on power chords, virtuoso leads and a heavy backbeat.

traits.v: Overdriven power chords and sustained lead guitar.
Heavy backbeat with blues-shuffle roots.
High, belted, blues-wailing lead.
Riff-verse-chorus with a guitar-solo centrepiece.

why: It weaponises the electric blues riff — louder, heavier and hook-first, the bridge between blues and metal.

tracks.why: A Chicago-blues riff detonated at stadium scale — the hard rock template.

name: Southern Rock
def: Blues rock played with Southern country phrasing and jam-band stamina — harmonised twin lead guitars, slide, boogie shuffles and solos stretched to fill a live set.

traits.v: Harmonised twin or triple lead guitars, bottleneck slide and Hammond organ.
Blues shuffle and boogie with a loping country lilt; double drummers in the Allmans model.
Verse-chorus openings giving way to long modal jams and traded solos.
Macon, Muscle Shoals and Jacksonville; Capricorn Records and the touring circuit.

why: It welds the electric blues riff to country phrasing and jazz-length improvisation — two leads moving in thirds over a shuffle, with the jam, not the hook, as the destination.

tracks.why: The Fillmore East reading — a blues in 11/4 stretched past twenty minutes of interlocking lead guitar.
A country-gospel ballad that detonates into a three-guitar coda — the genre's two halves in one song.

name: Heartland Rock
def: Straightforward American bar-band rock about working-class life — big open chords, Telecaster and organ, and plain-spoken narratives of small towns, factories and the road, peaking on FM radio from the late 70s through the 80s.

traits.v: Telecaster and open-chord rhythm guitar with Hammond organ, piano and harmonica over a square 4/4 backbeat.
Plain-spoken, rough-edged narrative voice singing character songs about ordinary lives.
Midwest and Rust Belt America — bar bands scaled up to FM radio and the arena.

why: It keeps rock 'n' roll's three chords and adds folk's narrative seriousness — working-class American storytelling played by a bar band, against the polish of its arena-era peers.

tracks.why: A 1982 No. 2 hit — bar-band riff, big backbeat and plain-spoken swagger, heartland rock at its chart peak.
Piano, harmonica and a small-town escape narrative — the genre's founding statement.

name: Arena Rock
def: Rock engineered for the stadium — huge choruses, power ballads and radio-polished production designed for twenty thousand voices singing along.

traits.v: Anthemic verse-lift-chorus with singalong hooks.
Big, layered, FM-radio gloss.
Spectacle — lights, pyro and the crowd as instrument.

why: It optimises hard rock for scale — every chorus a communal anthem, every ballad a lighter-waving set piece.

tracks.why: The slow-build power anthem perfected — engineered for mass singalong.

name: Yacht Rock
def: The smooth West Coast studio sound — session-perfect soft rock gliding on jazz chords, R&B grooves and immaculate late-70s production.

traits.v: Immaculate LA session polish.
Jazz-derived extended chords under pop hooks.
Relaxed, syncopated R&B-lite grooves.
Smooth, high, blue-eyed-soul harmony stacks.

why: It fuses soft rock with soul and fusion chops into a frictionless studio sheen — smoothness as the aesthetic itself.

tracks.why: McDonald's syncopated Rhodes hook is the cornerstone of the smooth sound.

name: Grunge
def: Seattle's collision of punk, metal and 70s riff rock — fuzz-caked, loud-quiet dynamics and throat-torn vocals that dragged the underground onto MTV.

traits.v: Thick fuzz and sludgy, detuned riffs.
Quiet verses detonating into roaring choruses.
Torn, howled, disaffected.
Sub Pop, Seattle and the 1991 breakthrough.

why: It fuses hardcore's economy with metal's weight and hard rock's riff — the underground's sound at mainstream scale.

tracks.why: Sub Pop's fuzz-caked signature single — grunge before the gold rush.

name: Proto-Punk
def: The raw, confrontational garage-and-art-rock bands who prefigured punk — minimal chords, nihilist attitude and abrasive energy.

traits.v: Driving, primitive eighth-note pulse.
Distorted, untreated guitar; deadpan or sneering vocals.
Underground art and street provocation.

why: Minimal distorted riffing and confrontational delivery strip rock toward the speed and attitude punk would formalise.

name: Punk
def: A stripped-to-the-bone rejection of rock excess — fast, short, confrontational and defiantly DIY. As much an ethos as a sound.

traits.v: Fast tempos and relentless downstroke eighths.
Two-minute, hook-and-shout verse-chorus blasts.
DIY labels, zines and anti-virtuosity.

why: It compresses rock to fast, short, confrontational bursts where attitude and speed replace musicianship.

tracks.why: Two-minute four-to-the-floor downstrokes proved a song needs only speed and a hook.

name: New Wave
def: Punk's energy made melodic and modern — synths, angular pop hooks and art-school style for the radio.

traits.v: Synths and drum machines alongside punchy guitars.
Bright, hooky, often nervy pop melody.
Clean, modern, radio-ready.

why: It keeps punk's brevity and nervous energy but adds synthesizers and polished pop hooks for the mainstream.

name: Noise Rock
def: Abrasive, dissonant guitar rock that weaponises feedback, atonality and distortion as the music itself.

traits.v: Detuned, atonal, feedback-saturated guitars.
Dissonance and noise over conventional chords.
Pounding, often math- or no-wave-derived.

why: Feedback and detuned dissonance are treated as primary material, foregrounding raw texture over melody.
tempoNote: Variable — tempo is secondary to texture and noise.

name: No Wave
def: A short-lived downtown New York scene that rejected rock's grammar outright — atonal slide guitar, free-jazz skronk, broken funk and deliberate amateurism.

traits.v: Atonal, unchorded, often deliberately untuned.
Jagged stop-start beats or warped punk-funk vamps.
Scraped, slide-played and skronking guitar and sax.
Lower Manhattan lofts, art galleries and the Eno-produced No New York.

why: It takes punk's anti-virtuoso stance further than punk did, discarding chords, song form and tuning in favour of free jazz's noise and confrontation.

tracks.why: James Chance's alto skronk over a rigid funk vamp shows no wave's punk-funk wing at its most danceable.

name: Alternative Rock
def: The umbrella for guitar bands working outside the mainstream — college radio, indie labels and a broad church of post-punk descendants.

traits.v: Loud-quiet-loud dynamics and unconventional forms.
Mid-fi, label-independent.
College radio and the 90s breakthrough.

why: It channels post-punk's sensibility into guitar bands whose loud-quiet dynamics broke into the mainstream.

tracks.why: Its loud-quiet-loud dynamic became the blueprint for a decade of alt-rock.

tempoNote: Wide range — an umbrella genre with no single tempo identity.

name: Indie Rock
def: Guitar pop defined by independent-label ethos — melodic, unpolished and personal rather than arena-scaled.

traits.v: Lo-fi to mid-fi, intentionally unglossy.
Jangly, hook-forward songwriting.
Independent labels and word-of-mouth networks.

why: It foregrounds songcraft and a deliberately modest, hand-made production over commercial sheen.

name: Space Rock
def: Hypnotic, effects-drenched rock built on repetition, drone and the imagery of flight — Hawkwind's amplified free-festival pulse in 1970, revived in the late 80s by Spacemen 3 and Loop as the bridge into shoegaze.

traits.v: Motorik, repetition-driven momentum.
Reverb and delay washes over droning synths.
Long, gradually evolving builds.
Ladbroke Grove free festivals and Hawkwind's light-show happenings, 1970 on; the Rugby-born Spacemen 3 revival from 1986.

why: It fuses a steady, repeating pulse with cavernous, delayed guitar and synth drones to create weightless forward drift.

tracks.why: A one-chord riff, phased synth whoosh and chanted lift-off — the 1972 template every later space rock band restaged.

name: Post-Rock
def: Rock instrumentation used for texture and dynamics rather than riffs and verses — crescendos, loops and cinematic instrumentals.

traits.v: Long dynamic builds; quiet-to-cathartic arcs over verse-chorus.
Layered, treated, tremolo guitars; timbral focus.
Modal, suspended, slow-moving.
Strings, brass and glockenspiel beside guitars.

why: Guitars become timbral and dynamic tools for long crescendos, borrowing jazz and minimalism's patience over rock's hooks.

albums.t: Lift Your Skinny Fists Like Antennas to Heaven

tempoNote: Highly variable — long builds move through several tempos in one piece.

name: Gospel-Inflected Rock
def: Rock built on the musical grammar of Black American gospel — plagal cadences, choir stacks, organ and communal build — independent of any religious lyrical content. Not Christian rock, which is a market and content category rather than a sonic one.

traits.v: Plagal IV–I cadences and amen resolutions rather than dominant tension.
Call-and-response between lead and backing, with stacked choir or multi-tracked group vocals.
Hammond organ, upright and electric piano, tambourine, handclaps, horn sections in soul voicings.
Vamp-and-build — repeat a figure, add layers, never modulate.
Communal build to catharsis instead of verse-chorus contrast.

why: Borrowing the church's cadences, response singing and layered vamp gives rock a way to reach catharsis by accumulation rather than by contrast — the crowd, not the chorus, is the payoff.

albums.t: Ladies and Gentlemen We Are Floating in Space

tracks.t: You Can't Always Get What You Want
tracks.why: A choir, a horn section and a vamp that builds without ever resolving into a conventional chorus.

name: Hardcore Punk
def: Punk accelerated past its limits — faster, shorter, angrier, and built on a fiercely self-organised network of DIY labels, vans and all-ages shows.

traits.v: Breakneck tempos, D-beats and shouted unison drive.
Sub-two-minute blasts; no solos, no fat.
Barked, shouted, slogan-like delivery.
DIY labels, zines and the all-ages touring circuit.

why: It compresses punk to maximum velocity and moral intensity, and its DIY infrastructure becomes the template for every underground since.

tracks.why: A shouted group-chorus over relentless downstrokes — hardcore's defiance distilled.

name: Post-Hardcore
def: Hardcore's intensity opened up — dynamics, dissonance, melody and space let the fury breathe without losing its edge.

traits.v: Tension-and-release arcs instead of constant blast.
Angular, syncopated interplay of bass and guitar.
Shouts, spoken word and singing traded freely.
Dischord and the post-Revolution Summer D.C. underground.

why: It keeps hardcore's urgency but lets arrangements stretch, quiet down and turn dissonant — punk discovering dynamics.

tracks.why: Its coiled, dub-tense verse exploding into the chorus is post-hardcore's dynamic blueprint.

name: Emocore
def: Washington, D.C. hardcore remade in 1985's Revolution Summer — the same speed and volume, turned from macho aggression toward personal, poetic and openly emotional songs.

traits.v: Strained, pleading singing that breaks into a scream.
Hardcore drive with dynamic drops and improvised, collapsing endings.
Post-punk-tinged, chiming distorted guitars.
Dischord Records, Inner Ear Studios and the 1984–86 Revolution Summer.

why: It keeps hardcore's velocity but rejects its violent posturing, pointing the music at vulnerability — the seed of both emo and post-hardcore.

tracks.why: The 1985 recording that defined emotional hardcore before the word existed.

name: Ska Punk
def: 2 Tone's fusion rebuilt on American hardcore — breakneck skank verses, gang-vocal choruses and a horn section riding a punk rhythm section.

traits.v: Alternating hardcore blast and up-stroke skank.
Brass over distorted power-chord guitar.
Gruff lead with gang-shouted hooks.
East Bay and Southern California DIY punk, then mid-90s radio.

why: It welds 2 Tone's skank to hardcore's speed and gang-vocal delivery — the third wave, and ska's route onto US radio.

tracks.why: Hardcore and skank alternating bar to bar — the third wave's template in ninety seconds.

name: Skate Punk
def: Southern California hardcore given melody — the skate beat's double-time drive under sung leads and stacked harmonies, built around Epitaph and Fat Wreck Chords and taken mainstream by The Offspring's Smash in 1994.

traits.v: The "skate beat": double-time polka drumming with the snare on every offbeat.
Melodic sung leads over stacked "oohs" and three-part backing harmonies.
Tight palm-muted power chords with short melodic leads.
Epitaph, Fat Wreck Chords, skate videos and the Warped Tour.

why: It keeps hardcore's tempo and DIY network but puts a sung melody and choir-like harmonies on top — the template the 90s pop-punk boom grew from.

tracks.why: Skate-beat drums, palm-muted verses and a sung hook — the Fat Wreck sound in two and a half minutes.

name: Pop-Punk
def: Punk's speed and power chords set to bubblegum hooks — rooted in the Ramones, Buzzcocks and Descendents, made a mass-market genre by Green Day's Dookie in 1994 and carried into the 2000s by Blink-182 and the emo-pop wave.

traits.v: Singalong major-key hooks; the chorus is the point.
Skate-beat verses dropping into straight, mid-tempo choruses.
Nasal, conversational singing about boredom, adolescence and heartbreak.
Bright, tight, radio-ready guitars and drums.

why: It slows skate punk a notch and pushes the hook to the front, turning punk into teenage pop without losing the distorted guitars.

tracks.why: Three chords, a skate-beat chorus and a confession about anxiety — the song that took pop-punk to MTV.

name: Emo
def: Hardcore's fury turned inward — confessional lyrics and soaring, melodic catharsis, born in D.C.'s Revolution Summer and broken open by the mid-90s second wave.

traits.v: Cracked, impassioned singing that tips into a yell.
Soaring, bittersweet lines over driving guitars.
Quiet-loud builds to cathartic climaxes.
From Rites of Spring's D.C. to 90s basement shows.

why: It keeps post-hardcore's dynamics and drive but aims them at the diary page — vulnerability delivered at full volume.

tracks.why: Its hushed verse erupting into a cracked, soaring chorus set the second-wave template.

name: Screamo
def: Emo pushed to its breaking point — shrieked vocals, chaotic dynamics and short, cathartic songs swinging between fragile quiet and total collapse.

traits.v: Throat-shredding screams over whispered passages.
Blasts, sudden stops and free-falling tempo shifts.
Compressed arcs from fragile to annihilating.
Basements, split 7-inches and screen-printed sleeves.

why: It takes emo's catharsis literally — the voice breaks into a scream and the song form shatters with it.

tracks.why: Whispered arpeggios collapsing into shrieked catharsis — the screamo arc in one song.

tracks.t: And You're Wondering How a Top Floor Could Replace Heaven

tempoNote: Highly variable — sudden stops and free-falling tempo shifts are the point.

name: Math Rock
def: Rock's rhythm section as puzzle box — odd meters, stop-start riffs and tapped, interlocking guitar figures played with surgical precision.

traits.v: Shifting odd meters — 7/8 into 11/8 without blinking.
Clean, tapped, interlocking guitar counterpoint.
Through-composed riff sequences over verse-chorus.
Chicago, Louisville and the Touch and Go orbit.

why: It treats the riff as an engineering problem — meters shift constantly and precision itself becomes the expressive point.

tracks.why: Looping, tapped guitar cells locking over shifting meters — math rock's method in full.

tempoNote: Range is nearly meaningless — constant odd-meter and tempo changes define the genre.

name: Britpop
def: Mid-90s British guitar pop reclaiming the Kinks–Beatles–Smiths songbook — big hooks, unhidden regional accents and wry English character studies, sold as the national answer to grunge.

traits.v: Singalong, chart-ready hooks built on 60s British beat and mod pop.
Regional accents worn openly; arch, observational narration.
Jangle and crunch guitars, Hammond organ, brass and string flourishes.
Camden, the music weeklies and the 1995 Blur vs Oasis chart war.

why: It rebuilds 60s British songcraft through post-Smiths indie, trading grunge's angst for chart hooks and very English storytelling.

tracks.why: Class satire over a relentless singalong build — the genre's sharpest song.

name: Math-Pop
def: Math rock's tapped, interlocking guitars and shifting meters folded into hooky indie songs — odd-time precision you can dance to. Mid-2000s Oxford, around Youthmovies and early Foals, is its clearest home.

traits.v: Clean, high-neck tapped guitar cells locking like sequencer patterns.
Odd meters and syncopated hi-hats, dance-punk tight.
Sung melodic hooks over the counterpoint.
Oxford's house-party and Truck Festival circuit; UK labels like Big Scary Monsters.

why: It keeps math rock's interlocking precision but points it at the chorus and the dancefloor.

tracks.why: Tapped guitar loops over a dance-punk hi-hat — Oxford math-pop at its most immediate.

name: Midwest Emo
def: Emo relaxed into Midwest basements — twinkly, tapped arpeggios, loose math-inflected meters and conversational confession at porch-light volume.

traits.v: Clean, twinkling, open-tuned arpeggios.
Loose, math-inflected meters at a lope.
Plain-spoken, cracked, half-shouted confession.
Trumpet and brushed drums beside guitars.

why: It swaps emo's roar for intimacy — math rock's guitar language slowed into bittersweet, autumnal songcraft.

tracks.why: Twinkling interlocked riffs in shifting meter — the most imitated song in emo.

name: Mathcore
def: Math rock's metric chaos detonated at hardcore intensity — atonal riffs, whiplash meter changes and screamed vocals in constant free-fall.

traits.v: Whiplash meter changes and blastbeat bursts.
Atonal, dissonant riff clusters.
Screamed, percussive — another instrument in the chaos.

why: It fuses math rock's shifting grids with metallic hardcore's violence — complexity weaponised rather than admired.

tracks.why: Whiplash meter chaos at hardcore violence — the track that defined the genre outright.

tracks.t: Saint Matthew Returns to the Womb

tempoNote: Range is nearly meaningless — whiplash meter and tempo chaos is the genre.

name: Emo Revival
def: A 2010s generation raised on Midwest emo brings it back — twinkly guitars, group-shout climaxes and sprawling, sincere songwriting for the DIY-streaming era.

traits.v: Twinkly arpeggios beside post-rock swells.
Group shouts and unguarded, wordy confession.
Bandcamp, DIY houses and festival reunions.

why: It reclaims second-wave and Midwest emo's sincerity wholesale, scaled up with post-rock dynamics and internet-era reach.
artists: The World Is a Beautiful Place & I Am No Longer Afraid to Die

albums.a: The World Is a Beautiful Place & I Am No Longer Afraid to Die

tracks.a: The World Is a Beautiful Place & I Am No Longer Afraid to Die
tracks.why: Its swelling group-shout finale is the revival's communal thesis.

name: Desert Punk
def: Desert rock's fuzz stripped back to punk velocity — scuzzy, skate-culture DIY bands playing generator-party riffs at hardcore speed.

traits.v: Fast, driving punk tempos under heavy fuzz.
Blown-out, sun-bleached garage distortion.
Skate videos, DIY shows and desert campouts.

why: It runs the desert's fuzzed riff language at punk speed — Kyuss groove with a hardcore engine.

tracks.why: Skate-punk velocity through a desert fuzz stack — the fusion in one blast.

name: Folk Rock
def: Folk repertoire and songwriting played by an electric rock band — chiming twelve-string guitar, close harmony and traditional or topical lyrics over drums and bass.

traits.v: Twelve-string electric guitar, bass and drums beside acoustic and fiddle.
Close, blended harmony carrying narrative or traditional lyrics.
Strophic ballad forms held intact inside a rock arrangement.
1965 Los Angeles — the Byrds, the Mamas & the Papas and, by 1969, CSNY and Joni Mitchell in Laurel Canyon — and, from 1969, the British trad revival.

why: It electrifies the folk revival without discarding it — the ballad and its lyric survive intact while a rhythm section and ringing twelve-string carry them.

tracks.why: McGuinn's twelve-string Rickenbacker over a Dylan lyric is the founding sound of the genre.
A centuries-old English ballad driven by a rock rhythm section — the British trad wing in one track.

name: Synth Pop
def: Pop rebuilt entirely on the synthesizer — sequenced basslines, drum machines and glossy hooks that carried post-punk's machines onto the charts.

traits.v: All-electronic: sequencers, drum machines, polysynths.
Bright, hooky pop lines over a machine pulse.
Clean, quantised, radio-ready gloss.
Post-punk UK gone pop-chart.

why: It replaces the rock band wholesale with sequencers and drum machines while keeping pop's hooks intact.

tracks.why: An all-synth chart-topper that proved the synthesizer could replace the band.

name: Madchester
def: Manchester's indie-dance collision — jangling psychedelic guitar pop swung onto acid house's groove, born of the Haçienda and ecstasy culture.

traits.v: Funky, loose-limbed dance drumming under guitar pop.
Wah and jangle guitar over baggy breakbeats.
The Haçienda, rave culture and baggy fashion.

why: It puts indie guitar bands on the dancefloor — psychedelic jangle riding acid house's rhythm section.

tracks.why: Ten minutes of funk breakbeat under psychedelic guitar — the indie-dance fusion in full.

name: Jangle Pop
def: Chiming, clean arpeggiated guitar pop — 60s folk-rock's 12-string ring revived through post-punk's economy and indie's modesty.

traits.v: Bright, clean, arpeggiated electric guitar; no distortion.
Wistful, melodic, harmony-rich songcraft.
College radio and UK indie 45s.

why: Its ringing, undistorted arpeggios put melody and chime where rock had put riffs and fuzz.

tracks.why: Marr's cascading arpeggios are the definitive jangle guitar statement.

name: Indie Pop
def: Melodic guitar pop made on a DIY footing — jangling guitars, a love of 60s pop and deliberately unpolished playing, set against mainstream pop's gloss. Named as a genre by NME's C86 tape in 1986, with roots in Glasgow's Postcard Records (1979) and the Television Personalities.

traits.v: Clean, jangling guitar; later strings, brass and glockenspiel.
Soft, untrained voices, often boy-girl harmonies.
60s girl-group and bubblegum hooks in short songs.
Fanzines and 7-inch labels — Postcard, 53rd & 3rd, Sarah. A Glasgow axis runs from Orange Juice to the Pastels, Belle and Sebastian and Camera Obscura.

why: It keeps punk's DIY ethic but trades its aggression for sweetness — modest, melodic and openly sentimental where indie rock is abrasive.

albums.t: Up for a Bit with The Pastels

tracks.why: Stephen Pastel's untrained vocal over scrappy jangle — the C86 sound at its most direct.

tracks.t: The Boy with the Arab Strap
Lloyd, I'm Ready to Be Heartbroken

name: Acid Rock
def: The heavier, jam-based end of first-wave psychedelia — garage psych, San Francisco ballroom rock and psychedelic blues-rock built on extended improvisation and volume.

traits.v: Open-ended jams stretching songs past the ten-minute mark.
Fuzz, feedback and modal lead guitar at ballroom volume.
San Francisco ballrooms, garage bands and the blues-rock power trio.

why: Psychedelia's studio trip taken to the stage — blues forms blown open by volume, improvisation and lysergic intent.

tracks.why: Ballroom psych distilled — a bolero build to a lysergic punchline.

tempoNote: Variable — extended jams speed up and dissolve.

name: Heavy Psych
def: Acid rock pushed to physical extremes — overdriven amp stacks, slow riffs and rhythm sections that traded finesse for sheer weight; the missing link to metal and stoner rock.

traits.v: Saturated amp distortion as the core sound, not an effect.
Heavy, dragging riffs and pummeling drums.
Post-Hendrix power trios chasing volume — the proto-metal underground.

why: When the jam bands turned everything up past clean, the riff replaced the raga — and metal's vocabulary was born.

tracks.why: Volume itself as the instrument — proto-metal in 1968.

tempoNote: Wide range — dragging sludge to overdriven freakouts.

name: Funk Rock
def: Rock riffing welded to funk's rhythm section — syncopated bass and drums under distorted guitar, from Band of Gypsys to the alternative era.

traits.v: Slap and syncopated bass locked with a rock backbeat.
Distorted riff guitar over clipped funk comping.
Shouted, rhythmic delivery riding the groove.

why: Hendrix's Band of Gypsys proved a rock guitar could sit on a funk pocket — a blueprint bands have re-run ever since.

tracks.why: The founding groove of funk rock — riff and pocket as equals.

name: Art Rock
def: Rock treated as fine art — conceptual albums, theatrical personae and avant-garde technique imported from the art school into the stage show.

traits.v: Concept-driven albums and suites over verse-chorus habit.
Studio-as-instrument arrangements; sax, synth and treated guitar.
Mannered, persona-driven delivery.
Art-school London and glam-adjacent avant-garde.

why: It imports conceptual thinking into rock — the persona, the staging and the album itself become the artwork.

albums.t: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust

tracks.why: Art-school collage as a hit single — glamour, irony and the avant-garde in three minutes.

tempoNote: Variable — theatrical ballads to motorik drive.

name: Glam Rock
def: Early-70s British rock in glitter and platform boots — stomping rock 'n' roll beats, big terrace-chant choruses and androgynous, theatrical personae built for Top of the Pops.

traits.v: Stomping, handclap-heavy backbeat revived from 50s rock 'n' roll.
Short, chantable hooks and singalong choruses.
Glitter, makeup, costume and gender play as part of the song.

why: It makes image and persona part of the record — the template for every rock act that treated the stage show as the point.

albums.t: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust

tracks.why: Chuck Berry boogie slowed to a sultry strut — glam's founding hit.

name: Baroque Pop
def: Mid-60s pop ornamented with the conservatory — harpsichords, string quartets, horns and counterpoint wrapped around melancholy songcraft.

traits.v: Harpsichord, strings, woodwinds and orchestral colour.
Chromatic, classically-voiced progressions.
Bittersweet, through-written vocal lines.

why: It proved the pop single could carry orchestral harmony and formal ambition — the direct ancestor of every chamber-inclined songwriter since.

tracks.why: French horn, contrapuntal vocals and unresolved harmony — the baroque pop pinnacle.

name: Electronic Rock
def: Rock built around oscillators, early synthesizers and tape electronics rather than guitar alone — an umbrella that runs from 1968 experiments to today's synth-driven bands.

traits.v: Oscillator drones, primitive synths and tape effects in a band setting.
Repetitive, often machine-like pulse under a rock frame.
Late-60s New York and LA experimental underground.

why: It proved electronics could be a rock band's core instrument, opening the path to synth-pop, new wave and industrial rock.

tracks.why: Homemade oscillators and drums — electronics as the lead instrument of a rock song.

name: Industrial Rock
def: Industrial's machine noise and samples welded to rock songwriting — distorted guitars, drum programming and aggressive vocals.

traits.v: Sampled metal percussion, distorted synths and guitars.
Sequenced, mechanical drum programming.
Late-80s Chicago Wax Trax! scene into 90s alternative radio.

why: It carried industrial's harshness into song form and onto mainstream alternative radio.

tracks.why: Industrial programming under a pop-structured rock chorus.

name: Indietronica
def: Indie songwriting framed by laptop production, glitchy beats and warm synths — bedroom electronics with a band's sensibility.

traits.v: Laptop sequencing, glitch textures and IDM-derived beats.
Soft, intimate indie vocals.
Late-90s and 2000s indie labels; peaks mid-2000s.

why: It brought IDM's production into indie pop, setting up the 2000s electropop and bedroom-pop sound.

tracks.why: Glitchy laptop beats under a plainly indie pop song.

name: Indie Dance
def: Post-punk’s scratchy guitars pointed at the dancefloor — live bands playing disco and house rhythms with punk attitude and cowbell.

traits.v: Four-on-the-floor and disco hi-hats played by a live band.
Scratchy funk guitar, analogue synth stabs, cowbell.
DFA-era New York and the mid-00s indie disco.

why: It re-fused the post-punk/disco split of 1979, letting guitar bands work dancefloor dynamics without machines.

tracks.why: The DFA-produced shriek-funk single that relit dance-punk.

tracks.t: Daft Punk Is Playing at My House

name: Grunge Gaze
def: 90s alt-rock heaviness dissolved into shoegaze wash — detuned Seattle riffs under dreamy, reverb-smeared vocals. A 2010s wave that became a defining 2020s frontier.

traits.v: Downtuned grunge guitars under gauzy shoegaze reverb.
Soft, buried melody over heavy backing.
2010s heavy-gaze bands feeding TikTok-era 90s nostalgia.

why: It splices grunge’s weight to shoegaze’s blur — loud-quiet catharsis delivered as texture instead of scream.

tracks.why: The 2016 record that proved detuned grunge weight and gaze blur belong together.
Alice in Chains heaviness sung like Slowdive — the hybrid in one track.

name: Ambient Post-Rock
def: Post-rock with the climax removed — guitar swells, e-bow drones and reverb architecture drifting at ambient patience.

traits.v: E-bowed, reverb-stacked guitar as pure atmosphere.
Slow swells and dissolves; no drop, no chorus.
Often beatless or rubato — pulse implied, not stated.

why: It keeps post-rock’s guitar language but trades the crescendo for stillness — rock instrumentation, ambient time.

tracks.why: The band’s beatless side became a genre — swells as the whole story.

tempoNote: Often rubato — swells matter more than the grid.

name: Bedroom Pop
def: Intimate, lo-fi pop self-produced in bedrooms — soft vocals close to the mic, woozy guitars and laptop drums, distributed straight to streaming.

traits.v: DIY laptop recording; hiss and room tone kept in.
Whispered, conversational closeness.
SoundCloud, Bandcamp and YouTube as the label.

why: Cheap recording plus direct distribution collapsed the studio system — intimacy itself became the aesthetic.

tracks.why: A webcam video and a laptop beat reaching millions — the genre’s origin story.

name: Alternative Pop
def: Mainstream pop turned dark and downbeat — minimal, bass-heavy production, close whispered vocals and melancholic, world-weary lyrics.

traits.v: Sparse, sub-bass-led, headphone-intimate mixes.
Breathy, close-mic, often whispered.
Minor-key, moody, unresolved.

why: It takes art pop's auteur control and trip-hop's nocturnal space into the charts, with electropop's machines stripped down to near-silence.

albums.t: When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go?

tracks.why: Finger snaps, sub bass and a deadpan voice: chart pop with almost nothing in it.

name: Noir Crooner
def: Early-60s ballad pop replayed as film noir. Roy Orbison's operatic croon, Spector echo and girl-group chord changes are set to songs about death, longing and haunted romance, sung by a reverb-soaked baritone over twangy guitar.

traits.v: Baritone or operatic croon, often swooping into falsetto at the climax.
Deep spring and plate reverb, tremolo guitar, slapback echo.
Doo-wop and girl-group progressions (I–vi–IV–V) tilted toward minor keys.
Lynchian Americana: dim lounges, desert highways, Halloween and the graveyard.

why: It keeps the pre-Beatles ballad's croon and echo but darkens the lyrics and slows the tempo, so the 1961 prom slow-dance becomes a ghost story.

tracks.why: Tremolo guitar, a falsetto lament and David Lynch's patronage set the template in 1989.

name: Traditional Pop
def: Pre-rock popular song built on Tin Pan Alley and Broadway standards: a featured singer in front of an orchestra, phrasing the lyric close to the microphone.

traits.v: Close-mic croon or full operatic projection, with the lyric at the centre.
String orchestra or big band, written by a named arranger (Nelson Riddle, Gordon Jenkins).
32-bar AABA standards ending on a held note.
Radio, nightclubs and the long-playing album.

why: It made the singer the star and the ballad the main event, the starting point for every crooner since.

tracks.t: In the Wee Small Hours of the Morning
tracks.why: A 1955 album of late-night ballads: the noir mood in its first form.

tempoNote: Wide range — slow ballads to swinging up-tempo numbers.

name: Nu-Yacht Rock
def: Yacht rock’s studio perfectionism revived sincerely — smooth Rhodes changes, immaculate session playing and West Coast gloss for the streaming era.

traits.v: Major-7th and slash-chord smoothness, played straight.
Warm, analogue-styled, session-grade polish.
Crate-digger reverence meeting soft-rock rehabilitation.

why: A generation raised on irony re-learned the craft behind the smoothness — revival as studied musicianship, not pastiche.

tracks.why: Kenny Loggins and Michael McDonald guesting — the torch literally passed.

name: Soft Rock
def: The mellow, melodic mainstream of early-70s rock — acoustic guitars and electric piano, smooth lead vocals and layered harmony, produced for AM radio and the living room rather than the arena.

traits.v: Smooth, unforced lead with lush backing harmony.
Acoustic and clean electric guitar, Wurlitzer or piano, light strings.
Clean, balanced, radio-friendly — no distortion, no excess.
Verse–chorus with a strong hook and a key change or modulation for the last chorus.

why: It takes folk rock's acoustic warmth and sunshine pop's harmony singing and removes every rough edge, so melody and vocal blend are all that remain.

tracks.why: A 1970 No. 1 that set the template — hushed vocal, acoustic strum and strings with nothing abrasive anywhere.

tracks.t: (They Long to Be) Close to You

tempoNote: Unhurried ballads and easy mid-tempo — 'Dreams' sits around 120 but feels slower.

name: Australian Pub Punk
def: The Australian line that ran Detroit proto-punk through the beer-barn circuit — the Saints and Radio Birdman in 1976–77, then a blues-rotted swamp strain (the Scientists, the Birthday Party, Beasts of Bourbon) that persists in the Drones, Tropical Fuck Storm and Amyl and the Sniffers.

traits.v: Overdriven, trebly guitars; from the 80s, slide, tremolo and swamp-blues sludge.
Flat-out downstroke punk or a lurching, tom-heavy swamp stomp.
Snarled, drawled or howled — Australian accent unhidden.
Brisbane, Sydney, Perth and Melbourne pubs; isolation from UK and US scenes, with the Birthday Party exporting the sound to London in 1980.

why: Geographic isolation meant the Stooges, MC5 and blues records were absorbed without punk's fashion, so the result is heavier, swampier and more hostile than its UK or New York cousins.

tracks.why: Self-released in Brisbane in September 1976, before the Damned or the Pistols had a record out — the first punk single from outside the US.

tempoNote: Two speeds: Saints/Birdman punk tempo and the slow, dragging swamp lurch of the Scientists and Beasts.

name: Canterbury Scene
def: The English jazz-rock strain that grew out of one Canterbury friendship circle — fuzz-boxed organ and electric piano leading instead of guitar, shifting odd meters over a light jazz pulse, suite-length pieces, and wry, understated lyrics about golf, tea and the weather. Named for a place, defined by a sound; its membership has been argued over ever since.

traits.v: Odd and shifting meters — 7/4, 11/8 — carried lightly, with a jazz drummer's touch rather than rock weight.
Extended jazz chords and modal vamps under long instrumental suites; tunes modulate mid-phrase.
Fuzz-boxed Lowrey and Hammond organ, electric piano and saxophone take the lead; guitar is often absent.
Understated, conversational English singing — Robert Wyatt's high, plaintive tenor and Richard Sinclair's gentle croon — with whimsical, Dada-tinged lyrics.
The Wilde Flowers (Canterbury, 1964) split into Soft Machine and Caravan; the same players recombined for a decade in Hatfield and the North, National Health and Gong.

why: It plays jazz harmony and odd meters through a psychedelic pop sensibility, with the keyboard, not the guitar, as the distorted lead voice.

albums.t: In the Land of Grey and Pink

tracks.why: Wyatt's stream-of-consciousness vocal over nineteen minutes of fuzz organ and shifting meter — the whole style in one side of vinyl.

tempoNote: Highly variable — pieces change tempo and meter several times within a suite.

name: Avant-Prog / Rock in Opposition
def: Progressive rock's dissonant, politically engaged wing — through-composed chamber-rock pieces drawing on free jazz, Stravinsky and musique concrète, organised around Henry Cow's 1978 Rock in Opposition festival of bands the industry would not release.

traits.v: Atonal and polytonal writing, dense counterpoint, deliberate dissonance; melody rarely resolves.
Irregular, additive meters and abrupt tempo changes; grooves appear only to be broken.
Chamber-rock scoring — bassoon, oboe, violin and reeds alongside guitar, bass and drums; tape manipulation and studio collage.
Through-composed suites and improvised episodes rather than verse and chorus.
Henry Cow (Cambridge, 1968) and the March 1978 RIO festival with Univers Zero, Etron Fou Leloublan, Samla Mammas Manna and Stormy Six; a self-run, anti-industry network.

why: It keeps prog's compositional ambition but swaps its virtuoso pomp for modernist dissonance, free improvisation and political intent.

tracks.why: Fred Frith's angular theme in shifting meters, played by a rock band with the discipline of a chamber ensemble.

tempoNote: Wide range — through-composed pieces change tempo constantly; tempo is rarely a defining feature.
